passages.title: Signs in creation for people of certainty
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** This sūrah opens by naming where its message comes from — a Book whose revelation is "from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise" — and then, without pause, turns the reader's eyes outward to the heavens and the earth, inward to his own creation, and around him to the moving creatures, the alternation of night and day, the provision sent down from the sky, and the turning about of the winds. Ayat 3, 4 and 5 are three waves of the same argument, each ending by naming the kind of person who actually gets something out of it. Then ayah 6 closes the loop: what is recited to the Prophet ﷺ is called by the same name — the āyāt of Allah — so if a person will not believe in these, what speech is left for him to believe in?

## Where this sūrah stands

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this entire sūrah was revealed at Makkah except for one verse: according to one view, ayah 14 — "Tell those who believe that they should forgive those who do not believe in Allah's days" — was revealed at Madinah, with the rest revealed at Makkah. The overwhelming view, however, is that the entire sūrah was revealed before the hijrah (the Prophet's migration to Madinah).

That matters for how you read these opening lines. Like other Makkan sūrahs, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, its basic subject-matter is the basic beliefs of Islam: the Oneness of Allah, the messengership of the Prophet ﷺ, and the Hereafter. It adds that arguments and evidence have been adduced in favour of all the fundamental articles of faith — with evidence especially in favour of the Hereafter advanced — and that the criticisms of atheists and the fallacious arguments of the sceptics have been refuted elaborately. So this is not decoration. Ayat 3–5 are the opening move in a sustained argument, and the audience being argued with includes people who deny.

*(A note on the sources: the commentary volume in front of us carries over its closing lines from the previous sūrah — "the commentary on Surah Ad-Dukan ends here", together with a remark on those who "will not taste death therein, except for the first death", which is 44:56. That material belongs to the preceding sūrah, not to our passage, and is set aside here.)*

## Ayat 1–2: where the Book comes from

Ayah 1 is **Ḥā-Mīm**. It is worth being honest here: the commentary in front of us does not stop to interpret these letters. Ibn Kathir quotes them and moves straight on to what follows, and so should we.

What follows in ayah 2 is a statement about the Qur'an's origin: **"The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise."** Two of Allah's names — *al-ʿAzīz*, the Almighty, and *al-Ḥakīm*, the All-Wise — stand at the very front of the sūrah, naming the One the Book comes down from. As Ahl al-Sunnah have always held, we affirm the names Allah has given Himself as He revealed them, without likening them to anything in creation and without emptying them of their meaning. Hold them in mind as you read ayat 3–5, because Ibn Kathir will describe what follows precisely as a display of Allah's great power.

## Ayat 3–5: three circles of signs

Ibn Kathir titles his comment on this passage plainly: *A Directive to contemplate over Allah's Ayat.* Allah, he says, directs His servants to contemplate His favours and gifts, as well as His great power that is demonstrated by His creating the heavens and the earth and the various types and categories of creatures in them.

Notice how the passage moves in circles that widen, then come close, then start turning.

**First, the largest frame (ayah 3): "Verily, in the heavens and the earth are signs for the believers."** The whole structure — the sky above and the earth below. This is the sign anyone can see simply by standing outside and looking up.

**Second, the closest frame (ayah 4): "And in your creation, and what He spread (through the earth) of moving creatures."** The argument comes home. Before you point at the heavens, the ayah points at *you* — your own creation is placed in the same list of evidence as the sky and the earth. Then it looks outward again at the creatures spread through the earth. Ibn Kathir fills in what those creatures cover with a deliberately sprawling list: angels, Jinns, humans, animals, birds, beasts, carnivores, insects, and various kinds of sea creatures.

**Third, the frame that never stops moving (ayah 5).** Ayat 3 and 4 point at things that exist; ayah 5 points at things that keep happening, day after day, in front of you:

- **The alternation of night and day.** Ibn Kathir describes it as each following the other in succession, never ceasing to come, as decreed — one bringing darkness and one bringing light. The sign is in that steadiness: a rhythm that comes exactly as it has been decreed.
- **"The provision that Allah sends down from the sky."** The word chosen is striking. It does not say "water" here — it says *provision* (*rizq*). Ibn Kathir explains that Allah the Exalted sends down the rain from the clouds when it is most needed, and that He calls the rain "provision" because it is the resource that produces various provisions. That is, the rain is named after what it becomes. The next time you are anxious about sustenance, remember where the Qur'an locates it: sent down from the sky, at the time it is most needed, by Allah.
- **The reviving of the dead earth.** "And revives therewith the earth after its death" — Ibn Kathir glosses: after it was dry and had no vegetation or life of any kind. Ground that was finished, and then was not. In a sūrah where, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, evidence is especially advanced in favour of the Hereafter, that image is worth sitting with rather than reading past.
- **The turning about of the winds.** Ibn Kathir unpacks this one in loving detail: sometimes towards the south and sometimes towards the north; some easterly and some westerly; some bringing sea breezes and some blowing from the land; some coming at night and some by day. Some winds bring rain, some cause pollination, and some just revive the soul, while some others bear no benefit. The variety itself is the point — all of it turned about, none of it self-directing.

## The three closings — and why they climb

Here is the detail both commentaries fasten onto. Each of the three ayat closes differently:

- ayah 3: signs **for the believers** (*li-l-muʾminīn*)
- ayah 4: signs **for people who have faith with certainty** (*yūqinūn*)
- ayah 5: signs **for a people who understand** (*yaʿqilūn*)

**Ibn Kathir's reading.** He observes that Allah said first "are signs for the believers", then "who have faith with certainty", then "who understand" — thus, in his words, ascending from one honourable stage to what is more honourable and higher in grade. On this reading the three endings are a rising ladder: faith, then faith with certainty, then understanding. The signs are always there; what changes is the one looking at them.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān approaches the same three closings as a description of *who benefits*. The current verse, it says, points to the fact that only those people will be able to benefit who have faith. In the second case, it will be beneficial to people who might not immediately embrace faith, but who do develop certainty in their hearts that these signs point to the Oneness of Allah — and possibly that certainty will one day turn into faith. In the third case, it could benefit those who may be neither immediate believers nor firm in belief, but who have a sound heart to understand: if they search into the signs with deep insight, they will inevitably end up with faith and firm belief.

And then the sober note that closes the argument: people devoid of sound intellect, or unwilling to use it, will remain unconvinced even if thousands of evidences or arguments are put forward to them. The failure is not in the evidence.

The two readings sit together well — Ibn Kathir watching the believer climb from stage to stage, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān watching the outsider be drawn in.

**What the signs are arguing for.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose of ayah 3 and verses like it directly: to affirm the Oneness of Allah. The same argument appears in Sūrah al-Baqarah, ayah 164 — which Ibn Kathir quotes here in full as the parallel passage — where the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that sail the sea with what is of use to mankind, the water sent down that makes the earth alive after its death, the moving creatures of all kinds spread therein, and the veering of winds and the clouds held between the sky and the earth are all gathered as "signs for people of understanding". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in the two places there is a slight difference in the argumentation, and points interested readers to Imam Razi's *Tafsir Kabir*, where those finer points are discussed.

## Ayah 6: the two kinds of āyāt meet

"**These are the Ayat of Allah, which We recite to you with truth.**" Ibn Kathir explains that "these are the Ayat of Allah" is in reference to the Qur'an, with the proofs and evidences that it contains, and that "which We recite to you with truth" means that they contain the truth from the Truth — that is, from Allah.

Notice what has just happened to the vocabulary. Ayat 3–5 spoke of Allah's *āyāt* in the heavens, the earth, your own creation, the alternation of night and day, the rain and the winds. Ayah 6 now uses the very same term for what is recited to the Prophet ﷺ. On Ibn Kathir's reading, both carry proofs and evidences, and both come from Allah. The one who reads creation honestly and the one who receives the recited Book are being pointed to the same Source.

Hence the closing question, which Ibn Kathir renders as a challenge: therefore, if they do not believe in Allah's āyāt nor abide by them, what speech after Allah and His āyāt will they then believe in? The creation has been laid out as evidence. The revelation has been recited in truth. A person who turns away from both has not run out of evidence.

## Living it

**Contemplation is a directive, not a mood.** Ibn Kathir reads ayat 3–5 exactly this way: Allah *directs* His servants to contemplate His favours and gifts and His great power. That reframes something most of us treat as optional. Looking hard at the sky, at rain, at your own creation, and drawing the conclusion, is something being asked of you.

**Start with what is nearest.** Ayah 4 places *your own creation* at the head of its list, alongside the creatures spread through the earth. The most available evidence you will ever have is nearer than the sky.

**Let the provision from the sky settle your heart.** Ibn Kathir says Allah sends down the rain from the clouds when it is most needed, and calls it "provision" because it is the resource that produces various provisions. Rain on dry ground is an argument, not just weather.

**Check which ending applies to you.** Faith, faith with certainty, understanding — Ibn Kathir calls these ascending stages, each more honourable and higher in grade than the last. It is worth asking honestly which one describes your relationship with the world outside your window today.

**Do not blame the evidence.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's warning is bracing: someone devoid of sound intellect, or unwilling to use it, will remain unconvinced even if thousands of proofs are put before him. When faith feels thin, the answer is rarely more arguments; it is a more honest look at the ones already in front of us — and, as ayah 6 insists, a return to the recited āyāt of Allah.

passages.title: Woe to the arrogant mocker of revelation
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat draw a portrait of a single kind of person — the man who *hears* the Qur'an and still turns away, not out of confusion but out of pride — and then tell you exactly where that road ends. What holds the passage together is one continuous movement: a character sketch (ayat 7–9), the verdict passed on it (ayah 10), and the closing statement that the very Book he mocked was guidance all along (ayah 11).

It does not begin cold. Ibn Kathir, introducing the passage, notes the argument that leads into it: if people will not believe in Allah's ayat nor abide by them, *what speech after Allah and His ayat will they then believe in?* Once revelation itself has been dismissed, there is no higher court of appeal left. So the passage stops arguing with such a person and starts describing him.

## Who was this revealed about?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports several accounts of the background of ayah 7. Some traditions relate that it came down in connection with **Naḍr ibn Ḥārith**; others report it was about **Ḥārith ibn Kaldah**; and yet others hold it concerns **Abū Jahl and his comrades**. These reports are transmitted through Qurṭubī, and the sources do not settle on one.

Then comes a point of real interpretive wisdom. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that there is **no need to refer to a particular person** in order to determine the meaning of a Qur'anic ayah. The word **kull** (كُلّ), "every" — *woe to* **every** *sinful liar* — deliberately opens the description outward: it refers to every person who bears the characteristics of the men who may have been in the background of the revelation.

This matters for how you read the passage. It is not a historical grudge against three Makkan men who are long dead. The occasion of revelation, where it is known, shows you what the disease looked like in the flesh; the word *kull* tells you the diagnosis outlives the patient. Anyone who bears those same traits steps into the same description — and so a believer reads these ayat with a certain unease about himself rather than satisfaction about others.

## The portrait: أَفَّاكٍ أَثِيمٍ

**"Woe to every sinful liar"** — *waylun li-kulli affākin athīm*. What the commentary describes is not someone who once lied or once slipped, but someone in whom lying and sinning have become settled traits.

Ibn Kathir unpacks the pair as a whole character. This is one **who lies in his speech, often swears, who is worthless, who commits and utters sinful acts and statements, and who disbelieves in Allah's ayat.** Notice how much of that description runs through speech: he lies with his tongue, he swears oaths carelessly with it, he utters sinful statements with it. And the list does not stay at the level of manners — it ends at disbelief in Allah's ayat. In this portrait, the loose tongue and the closed heart belong to one and the same man.

## Hearing without hearing (ayah 8)

Ayah 8 is the most piercing line of the passage, because it removes every excuse.

**"He hears the ayat of Allah recited to him"** — Ibn Kathir notes that *tutlā ʿalayhi* simply means *being recited to him*. The information reached him. The sound entered his ears. He is not a man who never got the message.

**"then he persists"** — *thumma yuṣirr*. Ibn Kathir explains this as persisting **in his disbelief, his denial, his pride, and his rebellion.** Persistence is the key idea: this is not a first reaction that might soften, it is digging in. And the Qur'an names the engine driving it — *mustakbiran*, **with pride.** He is not held back by a lack of evidence. He is held back by an unwillingness to be lowered.

**"as if he had not heard them"** — Ibn Kathir: *as if he did not hear them being recited to him.* Read that slowly. The Qur'an does not say he did not hear; it says he behaves **as if** he did not. The hearing happened; the man simply carries on as though it never did. That gap between what reached him and what he did with it is exactly what he will be answerable for.

**"So announce to him a painful torment."** Ibn Kathir explains the command as: convey the news to him that on the Day of Resurrection he will have a **painful, severe torment from Allah.** The Prophet ﷺ is not told to argue further. He is told to deliver the notice.

## From ignoring to mocking (ayah 9)

Ayah 9 marks a further step down. It is no longer a man who merely refuses to listen — now he engages, and what he does with what he learns is worse than ignoring it.

**"And when he learns something of Our ayat, he takes them as a jest."** Ibn Kathir: if he learns anything from the Qur'an, **he disbelieves in it and takes it as the subject of jest and ridicule.** So knowledge, in him, does not produce submission; it produces material for jokes. He picks up a verse the way a man picks up something to laugh at.

And the punishment is fitted to the crime with precision. **"For such there will be a humiliating torment"** — *ʿadhāb muhīn*. Ibn Kathir states plainly that this is the **recompense for ridiculing the Qur'an and jesting about it.** Ridicule is an act of contempt: it places the mocker above the thing mocked. So the requital is not merely painful, it is *humiliating* — the pride that let him look down on revelation is answered by being brought low. He wanted the higher seat; he is given the lowest.

## From the Sunnah: how seriously the Qur'an's honour is taken

Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith that shows how far the Sunnah goes to protect the Qur'an from contempt. In the Ṣaḥīḥ, **Muslim** recorded from **ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ **prohibited travelling with the Qur'an to enemy lands, for fear that the Qur'an might be desecrated by the enemy.**

Sit with the logic of that. The believers were not the ones doing anything wrong — they were simply carrying the Book with them. But the mere *possibility* that it might fall into hands that would treat it with contempt was enough to forbid the journey. If the Sunnah closes a door that far upstream of the offence, consider the weight of the offence itself: sitting in a gathering where revelation is turned into a punchline, or repeating the joke, or laughing at it.

## The verdict (ayah 10)

**"In front of them there is Hell."** Ibn Kathir: all those who have these evil characteristics will end up in Hellfire on the Day of Resurrection.

There is a fine point of Arabic here that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises. The word **warāʾ** (وَرَاء) is *mostly* used in Arabic in the sense of **"behind,"** and *occasionally* in the sense of **"front."** Most commentators take it here in the sense of **"front,"** and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān translates it that way. However, some commentators take it in the sense of **"back/behind,"** and read the ayah as saying that those living in haughtiness and arrogance have the fire of Hell **trailing behind them.** (Both readings are cited via Qurṭubī.)

Either way the man is caught, and the two images are worth holding together. On the first reading, Hell lies **ahead** — it waits at the end of the road he is so pleased with. On the second, it is **behind him** — trailing after him, keeping pace while he struts.

Then the ayah strips away, one by one, everything he might have leaned on:

- **"And that which they have earned will be of no profit to them"** — Ibn Kathir: their **wealth and children** will not avail them. These are the two things a man builds a life on and measures his standing by. On that Day they return nothing.
- **"nor those whom they have taken as protecting friends besides Allah"** — Ibn Kathir: the **false gods** they worshipped besides Allah will not benefit them in the least. The word here is *awliyāʾ*, protectors and patrons — the very ones you take on precisely so that someone will stand up for you when things go badly. Their entire purpose fails at the one moment it was needed.
- **"And theirs will be a great torment"** — *ʿadhāb ʿaẓīm.*

## The last word: "This is guidance" (ayah 11)

Ayah 11 closes the passage by naming what all of this was about. **"This is guidance"** — *hādhā hudā* — and Ibn Kathir says this is **a reference to the Qur'an.**

That single sentence reframes everything before it. The Book that was recited to him in ayah 8 and mocked in ayah 9 was not an imposition, a burden, or a claim needing a hearing. It was *guidance* — the thing a lost person most needs. Everything catastrophic in ayat 7–10 is the record of what a man did with a rescue he was handed.

**"And those who disbelieve in the ayat of their Lord, for them there is a painful torment of Rijz."** Ibn Kathir glosses this torment as one that is **agonizing and severe.** And notice the phrasing the ayah chooses: not "the ayat of Allah" this time, but **the ayat of *their Lord*** — *rabbihim*. The relationship is named at the very moment it is being denied.

**A pattern worth noticing across the passage.** Follow the punishments as they accumulate: a **painful** torment (ayah 8), a **humiliating** torment (ayah 9), a **great** torment (ayah 10), and finally a torment of **rijz** that is **painful** (ayah 11). Each name answers something in the portrait — pain for the persistence, humiliation for the ridicule, and finally the sheer weight of it all. The description escalates because the conduct escalated.

## Living it

The passage does not ask a believer to identify enemies. It hands him a checklist.

**Guard the tongue.** Ibn Kathir's portrait is heavy with speech — lying, frequent swearing, sinful words and deeds — and it stands in the same description as disbelief in Allah's ayat. A man's speech is not a small corner of his religion; here it is the first thing named.

**Beware the ordinary version of "persists as if he heard them not."** Ayah 8 describes a man who hears the ayat and carries on unchanged. A Muslim can do a quiet version of this: hearing a verse recited, nodding at it, feeling nothing, and living exactly as before. The passage asks the honest question — when an ayah reaches me, does it *move* anything? And it names what blocks the movement: pride. Something in a person does not want to be told.

**Refuse to be part of the ridicule.** Ayah 9 makes jesting about the ayat of Allah a matter of *humiliating* torment, and the Sunnah, as Ibn Kathir cites it, guards the Qur'an's honour so carefully that even carrying it where it might be desecrated was forbidden. Whatever the gathering and whoever is speaking, the believer does not lend his laughter to it.

**Count what will actually count.** Ayah 10 names two great reliances — what a person earns and who will stand up for him — and voids both. Wealth, children and patrons are not condemned here; they are simply weighed, and found to carry nothing on that Day.

**Come back to ayah 11 and keep it in view.** *This is guidance.* The same Book stands in front of every person in this passage and every person reading it. What separates the two outcomes is not access. It is what a person does in the moment after he hears.

passages.title: The subjected sea and the believers' forbearance
passages.tafsir:
**In brief:** These four ayat make a single argument. Allah first reminds us that the sea — and then everything in the heavens and the earth — has been placed at our service purely as His gift (ayat 12–13). He then tells the Prophet ﷺ to instruct the believers to forgive, and to endure the harm of, those who *do not hope for the Days of Allah* (ayah 14). And He closes by returning every deed to its own doer (ayah 15). The gift comes first; the forbearance follows from it.

## One argument, not two

The thread running through the passage is **gratitude**.

Ayah 12 ends with "that you may be thankful." Ayah 13 says the whole gift "is all from Him." And when ayah 14 describes the people the believers are told to bear with — "those who hope not for the Days of Allah" — Mujahid glosses that description in a single line: **"They do not appreciate Allah's favors."**

So the passage does not switch topics halfway through. It moves from the favours themselves, to the failure to recognise them, to the believer's response to that failure — which is not retaliation, because, as ayah 15 says, the reckoning is already settled elsewhere.

## The gift: the sea, and then everything (ayat 12–13)

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah "mentions some of the favors He gave to His servants, such as subjecting the sea for their service."

The verb behind "subjected" is **sakhkhara** — rendered in the two translations before us as "subjected" and "subjugated." It does not describe a conquest we accomplished; it describes something Allah did *for* us. The ayah says so with two words: **bi-amrihi**, "by His command." Ibn Kathir glosses this as the command "of Allah the Exalted, Who ordered the sea to carry ships." The sea carries the ship because it was ordered to.

**"And that you may seek of His bounty"** — *wa li-tabtaghū min faḍlih*. Ibn Kathir reads this of "commercial and business transactions." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the phrase out further and offers three readings, all defensible:

1. The Qur'an's usual sense of "seeking His grace" is **exerting oneself in seeking one's livelihood** — honest work, plainly.
2. It may point to the **skill man has been given** to move boats and pilot ships across the surface of the water, so that commerce could be carried on across the globe.
3. It may have nothing to do with sailing at all. On this third reading, "subjugating the sea" means that Allah **created many useful things in the sea** and made it serviceable for mankind, so that people could draw out its minerals and other wealth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that contemporary science confirms the oceans hold far more mineral wealth hidden in them than the dry land does.

None of these readings crowds the others out. One short phrase covers the wage-earner, the navigator, the merchant, and the miner.

**"And that you may be thankful."** Ibn Kathir ties the thankfulness to something concrete: it is gratitude "for earning various provisions brought to you from far away provinces and distant areas through the sea." The ayah does not ask for gratitude in the abstract. It points at the provisions that reached you from far away, and at the sea that carried them.

Ayah 13 then widens the frame to its limit: *and He has subjected to you all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth*. Ibn Kathir itemises: "the stars, the mountains, the seas, the rivers and all that you use for your benefit; these are all from His favor, kindness and bounty."

Then comes the phrase the commentators dwell on — **jamīʿan minhu**, "it is all from Him." Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and pointed: **"Alone without partners in giving any of it."** *Minhu* is not merely a statement of origin; it is a statement of exclusivity. Every item on that list came from one source, with no co-giver to thank alongside Him. Ibn Kathir supports this with another ayah: *"And whatever of blessings you have, it is from Allah. Then, when harm touches you unto Him you cry aloud for help"* (16:53) — a verse whose two halves sit uncomfortably together, since the One forgotten in the blessing is the One called upon in the harm.

Ibn Kathir then cites a narration recorded by Ibn Jarir, from al-ʿAwfī, from **Ibn ʿAbbās**, on this same phrase: *"Everything is from Allah, and that is a Name from His Names. So it all comes from Him without rivals to dispute His authority; surely, this fact is completely certain."*

**"Verily, in it are signs for a people who think deeply."** The closing clause names the audience. The signs are set out in public — the sea, the stars, the mountains, the rivers — but the ayah reserves them for those who *think deeply*: reflection that is deliberate and sustained, not a passing glance.

## The response the gift asks for (ayah 14)

Ibn Kathir states the meaning of the next ayah directly: it "means, let the believers forgive the disbelievers and endure the harm that they direct against them."

He then places it historically. Drawing on statements collected from **ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah**, he explains that in the beginning of Islam the Muslims were ordered to observe patience in the face of the oppression of the idolaters and the People of the Scriptures, "so that their hearts may incline towards Islam" — patience aimed at winning people. However, when the disbelievers persisted in stubbornness, Allah legislated for the believers to fight in jihād.

### Two occasions of revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records **two narrations** about the cause of this ayah's revelation, and reports both rather than choosing between them (citing Qurṭubī and Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī).

**The first** is Makkan: a pagan in Makkah reviled Sayyidnā **ʿUmar** (may Allah be pleased with him), and ʿUmar intended to retaliate. This verse came down, asking the believers to forgive the unbelievers and endure the harm directed against them.

**The second** is Madanī. At the battle of **Banū al-Muṣṭaliq**, the Prophet of Allah ﷺ and his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) pitched their tent at a well called **Muraysiʿ**. ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites, was with the Muslims. He sent his servant to fetch water from the well, and the man was delayed. Asked why, the servant explained that one of ʿUmar's servants was sitting on the bank of the well and would let nobody draw until the water-skins of the Prophet of Allah ﷺ and of Sayyidnā Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) had been filled. Ibn Ubayy cynically quoted a proverb: *sammin kalbaka ya'kulk* — **"Fatten your dog and it will eat you up."** ʿUmar heard about it, armed himself with his sword, and went towards Ibn Ubayy. This verse was revealed on that occasion.

Both narrations involve the same Companion, and in both he is on the point of answering an insult when the ayah comes down.

**Can both be true?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two ways of synchronising them, if both chains of transmitters can be authenticated. Either the verse was originally revealed in Makkah, and then, when a similar incident took place at Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it and applied it to the second incident — something that often happened in cases of the causes of Qur'anic revelation. Or else Jibrāʾīl (peace be upon him) may have come down with the verse a **second time** at Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, reminding them that this was an occasion to act upon it. In the technical vocabulary of tafsīr this second possibility is called ***nuzūl mukarrar***, "repeated revelation."

### "The Days of Allah"

The ayah does not say "forgive the idolaters." It says: forgive those who *do not hope for* — in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering, *do not believe in* — **ayyām Allāh**, the Days of Allah. Two points of language:

**What the phrase means.** According to most commentators, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, *ayyām Allāh* refers to the **reward and punishment** that Allah will requite on the Day of Requital. The word *ayyām* ("days") is used abundantly in Arabic in the sense of **"turn of events."** So these are not calendar days; the phrase points to Allah's decisive requital.

**Why this description and not another.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the choice of wording. Describing them this way probably purports to say that the real chastisement awaits such people in the Hereafter — and because they do not believe in the Hereafter, the punishment will be **unexpected** for them. An unexpected torture is most excruciating; the torment will therefore be most harrowing. They will be recompensed and repaid fully for all their evil deeds, and so, in the words of the commentary, "the Muslims are not to bother about taking them to task for every little thing."

That is also the sense of the ayah's closing clause, **"that He may recompense people, according to what they have earned."** Ibn Kathir explains: if the believers forgive the disbelievers in this life, Allah will still punish the disbelievers for their evil in the Hereafter. Forgiving does not make the wrong disappear; it leaves the reckoning where it already belongs.

### Is this ayah abrogated?

Here the scholars genuinely differ, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out both positions.

**Some of the scholars maintain** that the rule of forgiving the disbelievers applied only before the revelation of the verse of jihād, and that when jihād was ordained, the rule of forgiveness in this verse was abrogated.

**Most research scholars, however,** express the view that this verse has nothing to do with the verse of jihād. On their reading, the verse sets down a **general social law**: that Muslims should not wreak vengeance for every little thing. Such a law is universally applicable in every age and situation, and is needed even at the present time — so it is not accurate to treat it as abrogated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a chronological argument: if the battle of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq is the cause of this verse's revelation, then the verses of jihād cannot be its abrogators, because they were revealed before that event.

## Why the believer can afford it (ayah 15)

Ayah 15 closes the passage: *Whosoever does a good deed, it is for himself, and whosoever does evil, it is against (himself). Then to your Lord you will be made to return.*

The two halves are balanced, and the prepositions carry the weight: the good is *li-nafsihi*, **for** the soul; the evil is *ʿalayhā*, **against** it. Whoever does wrong has done it against himself.

Ibn Kathir's comment on the final clause: "you will all return to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, when you and your actions will be displayed before Him. Then, He will recompense you for your deeds, good for good and evil for evil."

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer:

**Receive the world as a gift.** The sea, the stars, the mountains, the rivers, the provisions that reach you from far-away places — ayah 13 says it is all *from Him*, alone, without partners in giving any of it. Gratitude here is not a mood; it is simply seeing the situation correctly.

**Let the reflection be deliberate.** Ayah 13 reserves the signs for *a people who think deeply*. The signs are public; the seeing is not automatic.

**Absorb the insult rather than answering it.** Ayah 14 tells the believers to forgive and to endure harm — revealed, on both narrations, at the moment a Companion was about to answer an insult in kind. On the view of most research scholars it is a standing social law, not a repealed one: do not wreak vengeance for every little thing. Ayah 15 explains why that is bearable — evil done is against the one who does it, and all of us are returning to the same Lord.

passages.title: Israel's scripture, division, and the clear way
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat tell one story with two halves. Ayat 16–17 look back at a people who were given everything — Scripture, understanding of it, prophethood, good provision, honour above the nations of their time, and clear proofs — and who then split apart, not for lack of evidence but because of envy. Ayat 18–20 turn to the Prophet ﷺ and, through him, to us: *you* have now been placed on a clear way; walk it, and do not let the desires of people without knowledge pull you off it. The hinge word is **"then"** (ثُمَّ) in ayah 18 — history is being handed over.

## What the Children of Israel were given (ayah 16)

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that Allah here "mentions the favors He granted the Children of Israel, such as revealing the Divine Books to them, sending the Messengers to them and granting them kingship." Read the list slowly, because every item is a gift and every item will shortly be an argument against them:

- **al-Kitāb** — the Scripture itself.
- **al-Ḥukm** — rendered in the source not merely as "wisdom" but as *the understanding of the Scripture and its laws*. It is one thing to possess a revealed book; it is another to be given the understanding of what it means and of the laws it carries. They had both.
- **al-Nubuwwah** — prophethood. Messengers were sent among them.
- **Ṭayyibāt** — "good things," which Ibn Kathir explains concretely as "such as foods and drinks." Not only spiritual privilege; material provision as well.
- **Preference above the nations** — and note Ibn Kathir's careful limit: "of their time." The favour was real and it was historical, not a permanent title deed.

Then ayah 17 adds one more: **"And We gave them clear proofs in matters"** (*bayyināt min al-amr*). Ibn Kathir renders this: "We gave them evidences, proofs and unequivocal signs." And that is exactly the conclusion he draws from it: **"Therefore, the proof has been established against them."**

This is the quiet logic of the whole passage. Gifts are not neutral. Where the evidence has been made unequivocal, the case stands established.

## How a community with proof still splits (ayah 17)

The Qur'an's phrasing is precise and devastating: **they differed not until after the knowledge came to them.** The dispute did not come from confusion. It came *after* clarity. Ibn Kathir: "yet they differed among themselves after the proof came to them, out of transgression against each other" — the ayah itself names it as envy among themselves.

So the cause named here is not intellectual at all. It is moral. Two people can read the same clear verse and disagree, and the disagreement can be about the verse — or it can be about the two people. Ayah 17 says that in this case it was envy and mutual transgression.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens this and shows why it sits here.** Citing Bayān al-Qurʼān, it explains that these verses serve to confirm the messengership of the Final Messenger ﷺ, and that under this theme the Prophet ﷺ is being consoled for the persecution his enemies were carrying out against him. Two points are being made at once:

1. **The Book of Mūsā (peace be upon him) contains many clear prophecies about the advent of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.** The People of the Book were not short of evidence.
2. **Therefore their rejection of him was never an evidence problem.** In Maʿārif's words, "the Israelites rejected him not because there was any dearth of arguments, signs and Divine prophecies to support and establish his claim, but because of jealousy, love of the world and personal desires" — specifically, they did not like "the very idea that the Final Messenger ﷺ should have appeared from among the non-Israelites."

Feel the comfort in that for a man being mocked and opposed. The message is: *your argument is not weak; their hearts are unwilling.* Nothing has gone wrong with the proof.

**"Verily, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection about that wherein they used to differ."** Note the address — Ibn Kathir points out that "your Lord" is spoken to the Prophet ﷺ: *O Muhammad*. It is personal reassurance. And note that the settling of the dispute is *deferred*, not cancelled: Allah "will judge between them by His just judgement." Divisions that cannot be reconciled in this world will be sorted out with perfect justice in the next. That belongs to Allah; the servant's task is not to force the verdict early but to stay on the truth meanwhile.

## "Then We have put you on a way of commandment" (ayah 18)

Now the address shifts fully to the Prophet ﷺ: **"Then We have put you on a (legal) way of commandment. So follow you that."**

Ibn Kathir unpacks the command in the plainest terms: "follow what was revealed to you from your Lord, O Muhammad, there is no true deity except Him, and turn away from the idolators." Three things in one breath — cling to revelation, hold to pure tawḥīd (that there is no true deity except Him), disengage from those who set up rivals to Allah.

And he draws the line to us directly. Commenting on the Children of Israel's split, he writes: **"This Ayah contains a warning to the Muslim Ummah as well. It warns them not to take the path the Jews took nor adopt their ways."** Ibn Kathir says that this is precisely why the *sharīʿah* verse follows. Having just been shown a community that received revelation and then fractured, we are handed our own revelation and told: *follow it.* The remedy for the disease described in ayah 17 is the obedience commanded in ayah 18.

### What "a way of the Matter" tells us about earlier laws

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on a genuinely important question, and it is worth following carefully.

The religion of Islam, it explains, has two layers. First, **the fundamental articles of faith** — such as the Oneness of Allah and the Hereafter. These "are immutable and were imparted to every Prophet and his Ummah since the inception of man." Second, **the ordinances, laws and injunctions related to practical life.** These "were different for different Prophets and their people," and "kept changing according to the needs of time and exigencies of circumstances."

Maʿārif's reading is that "a certain way of the Matter (i.e. the religion)" in ayah 18 describes this second type — the practical laws. From this verse, it says, the jurists have ruled:

> The Ummah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ must, of necessity, follow the sacred laws of the Sharīʿah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. As for the sacred laws of the previous Sharīʿahs, this Ummah is **not legally bound** to them unless the Qur'an and Sunnah support or confirm them.

And that support or confirmation, Maʿārif says, may take one of two forms:

1. **Explicit endorsement** — the Qur'an and Sunnah may explicitly say that a certain law of a certain prophet must be followed by this Ummah.
2. **Approving mention without any hint of abrogation** — the Qur'an and Sunnah may speak highly and favourably about a certain law of a previous Ummah without hinting that it is abrogated for this Ummah. "This indicates that the law is applicable in the Sharīʿah of this Ummah also."

In either case, Maʿārif notes, "the previous law becomes part of this Sharīʿah, and as such this Ummah is legally bound to follow it." He adds that this much is sufficient for understanding the status of previous Sharīʿahs, and that the details are available in the books of Islamic jurisprudence — itself a useful lesson in knowing where a question is properly settled.

Practically, this saves the believer from two errors: importing earlier religious practices into Islam on the assumption that "it's all one religion," and, at the other extreme, imagining that Islam broke with everything that came before. The articles of faith are immutable and shared by every prophet; the practical law we are bound to is that of Muhammad ﷺ.

## "And follow not the desires of those who know not" (ayah 18)

The command to follow is immediately paired with a command *not* to follow. Notice what the Qur'an says is being followed. It is not their *arguments* — it is their **ahwāʾ**, their desires. And it identifies them as **"those who know not."** The ayah joins the two: desire on one side, absence of knowledge on the other.

That is why the pairing matters. A revealed way of commandment on one side; the desires of those who know not on the other. There is no third option offered here — you are either following what was revealed, or following desire.

## Two networks of protection (ayah 19)

Ayah 19 answers the practical calculation behind most compromises: *but they can do something for me.*

**"Verily, they can avail you nothing against Allah."** Ibn Kathir puts the question rhetorically: "what will the loyalty that the idolators give each other avail them?" — and answers, "all they will earn from their protecting friends is more loss, destruction and demise." Whatever protection is on offer from those who reject Allah is not protection at all; it is shared ruin arriving together.

**"Verily, the wrongdoers are protecting friends of one another, but Allah is the Protector of those who have Taqwa."** The ayah sets two systems of allegiance side by side, and uses the language of protection for both. Wrongdoing has its own solidarity; it is not lonely. But look at the asymmetry: on one side, many mutually dependent protectors who cannot save each other. On the other, **one** Protector, and He is Allah.

Ibn Kathir then draws out the movement each protection produces. Allah, as Protector of those who have taqwā, "will deliver them from the darkness to the light." By contrast, "all the false deities are the protecting friends of those who disbelieve, taking them out of the light to the darkness." Two directions of travel — and every alliance you make is quietly pulling you along one of them. Note also the condition attached: this protection is stated for **those who have taqwā**, those who are careful of Allah. The promise is real, and it is not unconditional.

## "This is a clear insight for mankind" (ayah 20)

The passage closes on the Qur'an itself. Ibn Kathir states plainly that "This" is **in reference to the Qur'an**.

**Baṣāʾir li-l-nās** — Ibn Kathir renders it "a clear insight and evidence for mankind." Note who it is addressed to: **mankind**, with no narrowing clause attached. Insight and evidence are set before people at large.

Then the ayah narrows: **"and a guidance and a mercy for people who have faith with certainty."** Guidance and mercy are not stated for everyone who reads, but for those who receive it with certainty. The insight and evidence are for mankind; the guidance and mercy land where there is certain faith.

This is the exact answer to ayat 16–17. The Children of Israel were given evidences, proofs and unequivocal signs — and those alone did not hold them together, because envy and mutual transgression got in first. Evidence establishes the case; by itself it does not produce faith. So the Qur'an comes as insight and evidence for mankind, and as guidance and mercy for those who have faith with certainty.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, and no more than the text supports:

**Treat your knowledge as a liability as much as a privilege.** Ibn Kathir's phrase about the earlier community — "the proof has been established against them" — follows directly from the fact that they were given evidences and unequivocal signs. Clarity received is a case established.

**Watch the real cause of religious division.** Ayah 17 does not blame ambiguity; it names envy and mutual transgression, and places the split *after* the knowledge had come. Before defending a position, it is worth asking honestly whether you are defending the truth or defending yourself. Ibn Kathir explicitly says this ayah is a warning to *this* Ummah not to take the path they took.

**Audit your loyalties.** Ayah 19 asks what your alliances can actually do for you before Allah — the answer given is that they "can avail you nothing against Allah" — and states Allah's protection for those who have taqwā. One protection moves people from darkness to light; the other moves them out of the light to the darkness.

passages.title: Denying the Hereafter and worshipping desire
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat take apart the mind of someone who lives as though this world were all there is. They begin with a question about justice — could the wicked and the righteous really end the same way? — and end with the answer that only Allah gives life, takes it, and gathers everyone for a Day that is not in doubt. Read in sequence, the passage sets the denial of the Hereafter beside the man who has taken his own desire as his god. Ayat 21–22 argue for the necessity of a Day of Requital; ayah 23 turns to the one who obeys his desire; ayat 24–26 quote the denier's slogan, his argument, and the reply he is given.

## Could the good and the wicked possibly end alike? (21–22)

Ibn Kathir opens by stating the principle plainly: **the believers and the disbelievers are never equal**, and he brings the parallel ayah, "Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of the Paradise. It is the dwellers of Paradise that will be successful" (59:20).

The Arabic in ayah 21 for "those who commit evil deeds" is *ijtaraḥū as-sayyi'āt*. Ibn Kathir glosses it as "those who commit and practise evil" — not someone who slipped once, but someone whose practice it is. The claim being refuted is that Allah would "hold them equal with those who believe and do righteous good deeds, *sawā'an maḥyāhum wa mamātuhum* — equal in their life and their death." Ibn Kathir reads this as covering both stages: treated equally "in the present life of the world and in the Hereafter."

Then comes the verdict, *sā'a mā yaḥkumūn* — "worst is the judgement that they make." Ibn Kathir explains what is being judged: "worst is the thought that they have about Us and about Our justice, thinking that We will ever make the pious and the wicked equal in the Hereafter or this life."

**A man who prayed all night on this one ayah.** At-Tabarani recorded, through Shu'bah from 'Amr bin Murrah from Abu Ad-Duha from Masruq, that Tamim Ad-Dari once stood in voluntary prayer through the night until the morning reciting only this ayah — "Or do those who earn evil deeds think that We shall hold them equal with those who believe and do righteous good deeds?" — and Allah's reply came back at him each time: *sā'a mā yaḥkumūn.* A whole night on one verse. It is worth asking why. The ayah is not only about somebody else's bad theology; recited in the dark it becomes a question a believer puts to himself: *which of the two am I, and am I quietly living as though it made no difference?*

## Why the Hereafter is not optional (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān on 21–22)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats these two ayat as a single rational argument that divine reward and punishment are *necessary*, and it builds the case from ordinary experience:

- No one in this world receives his full measure of reward or punishment. Generally, the unbelievers and evil-doers "wallow in wealth and lead a life of luxury," while the obedient servants of Allah live in poverty, hardship and misery.
- The crimes of the wicked are often not detected. Even when detected, more often than not the criminals are not apprehended. If they are apprehended, they swear oaths — "lawfully or unlawfully, truthfully or falsely" — and look for loopholes. One in a million might be punished, and that not fully.
- Meanwhile the believer who follows the Shari'ah strictly gives up wealth and pleasures he treats as unlawful, so he is "deprived of many a comfort and pleasure in this world."

Since people are not requited here in proportion to their deeds, Maʿārif argues, it follows necessarily that there must be another world where they are recompensed in full. Otherwise it would be absurd to call theft, robbery, murder and the rest crimes at all: a thief may acquire in a single night what a university graduate could not acquire in years of employment and hard work. Without the Hereafter and accountability, the thief would simply be the better-off man — and "no reasonable person would ever accept this position." To the objection that governments legislate severe punishments for criminals, the answer is that experience shows only the foolish criminals get caught; the clever habitual ones always find ways of escaping, and "the escape-door of bribery is always open for them."

So the Day of Requital, Maʿārif concludes, could be denied only by someone who concedes that there is no such thing as good and bad, or that whatever a person acquires by any means is absolutely rewardable. No one accepts that. What is left is the absurd position the Qur'an is quoting: that good and evil are distinct, yet the consequences are equal — worse, that the criminal should have a more comfortable life than the righteous and innocent. "There could be no greater degree of wrong than this."

**Ayah 22 supplies the missing half.** "And Allah has created the heavens and the earth *bi'l-ḥaqq*" — Ibn Kathir explains *bi'l-ḥaqq* here as **"in justice."** And the ayah continues, "in order that each person may be recompensed what he has earned, and they will not be wronged." Maʿārif reads this second ayah as completing the first: because reward and punishment are not given in full measure in this world, there must be a life after death where they are — and so the Day of Requital is necessary "in order to wipe out wrong and injustice."

And if someone asks *why not settle accounts here and now?* — Maʿārif's answer is one of the most steadying sentences in this passage: that is not in keeping with the divine wisdom of creation. Allah made this world "the domain of deeds and test-and-trial," not "the domain of requital." **Allah knows best.**

## The god who is worshipped without a temple (23)

Ayah 23 turns from the argument to the arguer: "Have you seen him who takes his own desire (*hawā*) as his god?" Ibn Kathir's definition is devastating in its simplicity — he is one "who abides by his lust, and whatever his lust portrays as good he implements it, and whatever his lust portrays as evil, he abandons it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious difficulty. No unbeliever claims that his desires are his object of worship. So how is this *worship*? The answer opens up a principle that runs through the whole religion: **the ayah indicates that "worship" actually means "obedience."** Anyone who undertakes to obey someone against the obedience of Allah has made that one his object of worship instead of Allah. Maʿārif applies it directly: people who "do not care what Allah has forbidden and follow their whims and fancies" have made their desires their god *in this sense*, "although they may not have uttered it by word of mouth."

Maʿārif also quotes a couplet by an ʿārif (a term for one who has been given knowledge of Allah — a person of spiritual insight), who calls the objects of desire *idols*: "My forehead has swollen by prostrating before the statues of beauty, although I claim to profess the religion of Islam." In this couplet, Maʿārif explains, the poet has portrayed selfish desires as statues: whoever takes his desires as his leader and follows them is as good as their worshipper, and that is why they are described as deities.

**What the sources relate on desire.** Maʿārif cites, by way of Qurtubi, that Sayyidnā Abu ʿUmāmah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Of all the deities worshipped under the firmament of the earth, the most detestable one in the sight of Allah is *hawā*, that is, selfish desires." And Sayyidnā Shaddād ibn Aws (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A wise person is he who keeps his desires under control and works for life after death; and sinful is he who runs after his desires and yet expects the best in the Hereafter." (Our source relays both through Qurtubi without naming a hadith collection, so they are given here as Qurtubi's citations.) Maʿārif adds the saying of Sayyidnā Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh Tustarī (may Allah be pleased with him): *"Your ailment is your selfish desires. And if you oppose them, it will turn into your cure."*

That last line is worth keeping. Desire is not merely a nuisance to be tolerated; it is named as the illness. And the medicine named is not exotic — it is opposing it.

## "And Allah left him astray upon knowledge" — the two readings

Ibn Kathir notes that *wa aḍallahu Allāhu ʿalā ʿilm* has **two meanings**, and he presents both rather than choosing one:

1. **Upon Allah's knowledge:** Allah knew that this person deserves to be misguided, so He left him astray.
2. **Upon the man's own knowledge:** Allah led this person astray *after* knowledge reached him and the proof was established before him.

Ibn Kathir adds that the second meaning includes the first, but not the opposite.

Then the faculties close down one by one: "and sealed his hearing and his heart, and put a cover on his sight." Ibn Kathir spells out each: **he does not hear what benefits him, understands not what would lead him to guidance, and sees not the evidence with which he can be enlightened.** This is why the ayah asks, "Who then will guide him after Allah?" — and Ibn Kathir pairs it with a similar ayah: "Whomsoever Allah sends astray, none can guide him; and He lets them wander blindly in their transgressions" (7:186).

The closing words turn to the listener: *afalā tadhakkarūn* — "will you not then remember?" The description of the sealed man ends in a call to take heed.

## "Nothing destroys us except time" (24)

Ibn Kathir identifies the speakers here as **Ad-Dahriyyah** — those who make *dahr*, time, the explanation of everything — together with the Arab idolaters who embraced their creed and denied the Resurrection. They say that there is only this life, some dying and others being born, with no Resurrection or Judgement. He also mentions the atheist philosophers who deny the Creator and hold that the world returns to its original form once every thirty-six thousand years and restarts its life-cycle again, a cycle repeated for infinity — which, he says, contradicts sound reason and the divine revelation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines the key word: *dahr* means "time from the beginning of the world to its end," and also "a very long period of time." And it lays out the worldview compactly: on this view life and death "have nothing to do with Divine will and command"; they happen under natural causes — limbs, organs and abilities diminish through constant use, matter dissolves and is destroyed, and that is "the be-all and end-all of human existence."

Allah's reply in the same ayah is not a counter-theory but an exposure: *wa mā lahum bi-dhālika min ʿilm, in hum illā yaẓunnūn* — "they have no knowledge of it." Ibn Kathir: "**they speculate and guess.**" The claim was not demonstrated; by the ayah's own verdict it was presumed.

**Why cursing time is forbidden.** Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by the two collectors of the Sahih, and by Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah the Exalted says: "The Son of Adam annoys Me when he curses Ad-Dahr (time), while I am Ad-Dahr. In My Hand are all matters; I cause the alternation of his days and nights." In another narration: "Do not curse Ad-Dahr (time), for Allah is Ad-Dahr."

Ash-Shafi'i, Abu 'Ubaydah and several other Imams of Tafsir explained it as follows: during the time of Jahiliyyah, when an affliction, a calamity or a disaster struck them, the Arabs used to say, "Woe to Ad-Dahr!" — blaming such incidents on time and cursing it in the process. But it is Allah who causes these and all things to happen. So when they cursed Ad-Dahr, it was as if they were cursing Allah Himself, since He truly causes all incidents to happen. That is why abusing Ad-Dahr was prohibited. Ibn Kathir calls this "the best explanation for this subject, and it is the desired meaning. Allah knows best."

**A point of creed, and a disagreement named.** Ibn Kathir states that Ibn Hazm and those of the Zahiriyyah like him made an error when they used this hadith to include *Ad-Dahr* among Allah's most beautiful Names. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: it does not necessarily follow from this that *ad-dahr* is one of the names of Allah; here Allah is referred to as *ad-dahr* metaphorically or figuratively.

There is a quiet lesson here for anyone who has ever muttered at "these times we live in," at bad luck, at a cruel year. Maʿārif puts it directly: the power the unbelievers describe as "time" is in fact the divine power, and when people curse or revile time for their adversities, "they are in fact directing their reproach to Allah." **Complaint aimed at time lands somewhere.**

## "Bring back our fathers" — and the answer (25–26)

Ayah 25 records their entire case. Ibn Kathir explains that when the clear signs are recited — the truth made plain to them and used as evidence against them, asserting that Allah is able to resurrect the bodies after they have perished and disintegrated — their reply is: "Bring back our fathers, if you are truthful!" Ibn Kathir glosses it: "bring them back to life, if what you say is true."

The Qur'an's own word for this is *ḥujjah* — their argument. That demand is all they bring.

Ayah 26 answers on three levels at once — "Say: Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then He will assemble you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt."

- **"Allah gives you life"** — Ibn Kathir: you are yourselves witnesses that He brings you to existence after non-existence. He recalls 2:28, "How can you disbelieve in Allah? Seeing that you were dead and He gave you life. Then He will give you death, then again will bring you to life." Therefore, he says, He Who is able to initiate creation is able to restart it, as well and more obviously — as 30:27 says, "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him."
- **"Then He will assemble you on the Day of Resurrection"** — this answers the demand directly. Ibn Kathir: when He resurrects you, it will be on and for the Day of Resurrection, not in this life; therefore "bring back our fathers" is groundless. He gathers the supporting ayat: "The Day when He will gather you on the Day of Gathering" (64:9); "For what Day are these signs postponed? For the Day of sorting out" (77:12–13); "And We delay it only for a term already fixed" (11:104).
- **"About which there is no doubt"** — Ibn Kathir: there is no doubt that it will come. And the ayah closes, "but most of mankind know not" — which, he says, is why they deny the Resurrection and discount the fact that the bodies will be brought back to life. He sets beside it: "Verily, they see it afar off. But We see it quite near" (70:6–7). They "discount the possibility that Resurrection will ever come, while the believers believe that its occurrence is easy and imminent."

## Living it

Read as a whole, the passage moves from a question to a portrait to a promise, and each stage asks something of us.

**Do not expect the ledger to balance here.** Maʿārif's answer stands: this world was made the domain of deeds and test-and-trial, not the domain of requital. Seeing the wrongdoer prosper is not evidence against Allah's justice; ayah 22 says the accounting is for the Day when each person is recompensed for what he earned.

**Watch what is really being obeyed.** Maʿārif's principle reaches further than the disbeliever it was said about: worship means obedience, and whatever a person undertakes to obey against the obedience of Allah has been put in the place that belongs to Allah alone — even if he never says a word of it aloud.

**Keep the hearing open.** On Ibn Kathir's second reading, the man of ayah 23 was led astray *after* knowledge reached him and the proof was established before him; the sealing of hearing, heart and sight follows in the ayah. That is the warning the ayah leaves standing, and it ends by asking: *afalā tadhakkarūn* — will you not then remember?

**Do not curse the age.** Blaming "time," fate or the era for our afflictions is the very language the ayah quotes — and, as Maʿārif says, such reproach is in fact directed at Allah, in whose Hand all matters are.

**Let the Day feel near.** They see it afar off; Allah says He sees it quite near, and the believers hold its coming to be easy and imminent. Tamim Ad-Dari stood a whole night with one ayah about it. There is no doubt about its coming — the only real question is which of the two groups in ayah 21 we will be standing with when it does.

passages.title: Every nation kneeling before its record
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat bring Sūrah al-Jāthiyah to its close — the commentary of the sūrah ends here — with a scene of the whole of humanity, nation after nation, down on its knees before Allah while the records of their lives are brought out and read. Ayah 27 states who actually owns everything and who will lose on the Day the Hour arrives; ayah 28 shows us the posture of that Day and the summons to the record; ayah 29 lets the record itself speak, and tells us who wrote it. The thread running through all three is a single claim: **the kingdom is Allah's, the accounting is exact, and nothing you did has been lost.**

## The answer to "nothing destroys us except time"

Earlier in this sūrah the deniers had said, "…and nothing destroys us except time" (45:24). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what they meant: *dahr*, time from the beginning of the world to its end, was for them the real cause of life, death, changing fortunes and the turning of the whole universe. Living and dying, on their view, had nothing to do with any divine will or command — bodies simply wear out with constant use, matter dissolves, and that is the be-all and end-all of a human being. No hereafter, no reckoning, no owner.

Ayah 27 answers exactly that: **"And to Allah belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth."** Ibn Kathir draws out the force of it — Allah is the King and Owner of the heavens and the earth, and the only Ruler over them *in this life and in the Hereafter*. The universe is not a machine grinding on by itself. It is owned property, and its Owner has appointed a Day.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a related caution here that is worth carrying with you. Because everything in fact happens by Allah's will and volition, reviling time is prohibited. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not revile time because time actually is Allah." When a person curses or reviles the times for the adversities that have befallen him, he is in reality directing his reproach at Allah — because the power the deniers described as "time" is in truth the divine power. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to add that this does *not* mean that *ad-dahr* is one of the names of Allah; Allah is referred to as *ad-dahr* here metaphorically or figuratively. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this teaching without naming a particular collection, so it is passed on here exactly as the commentary gives it.)

## Who are "the followers of falsehood"?

**"And on the Day that the Hour will be established, on that Day the followers of falsehood shall lose"** (27). Ibn Kathir identifies who is meant by *al-mubṭilūn*: those who disbelieve in Allah and reject the clear proofs and unequivocal evidences that He has sent down to His Messengers.

Notice the word *lose*. The verse does not say they will be defeated in argument on that Day; it says they will lose — like someone who staked everything on a position that turns out, when the Hour comes, to have had nothing in it.

## Ayah 28: what *jāthiyah* actually looks like

**"And you will see each nation humbled to their knees."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces *jāthiyah* to the root *juthuww*, meaning "to sit with the knees upon the ground." Sayyidnā Sufyān (may Allah be pleased with him) defined it more precisely still: to sit in such a way that only the knees and the toes of the feet rest on the ground.

Sit with that image for a moment. It is not the composed sitting of someone waiting his turn. It is the crouch of a person whose legs have gone from under him — weight forward on the knees, toes braced, unable to stand. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that this type of sitting will be *on account of awe, horror and fear*. Ibn Kathir says the same: kneeling, fearful of the tremendous calamity and events.

**Ownership above, knees below.** Set the two halves of the passage side by side. Ayah 27: the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, the only Ruler over them in this life and the next. Ayah 28: every nation on its knees. That is the whole relationship in two pictures — absolute ownership above, and creatures on the ground below it.

## When the Fire is brought forth

Ibn Kathir records a report about the moment this kneeling happens: it was said that this will occur when Hellfire is brought forth, for she will exhale once, and everyone will fall to their knees — including Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, whom Ibn Kathir names here as al-Khalīl. He will proclaim, "Myself, myself, myself! Today, I will not ask You (O Allah) but about myself." And even ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, will proclaim, "Today, I will only argue before You on my own behalf; I will not ask You about Maryam, who gave birth to me."

Ibn Kathir introduces this with "it was said," without naming a collection, so it is offered here at exactly that weight. But feel what it is saying. ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, will not raise the case of his own mother — the one who, in his own words in the report, gave birth to him. Not because he ceases to love her, but because on that Day every soul stands in its own place. If Ibrāhīm and ʿĪsā, peace be upon them, say "myself," then no one is coasting in on someone else's account: not on a pious father, not on a teacher he once studied with, not on a lineage.

## Does everyone kneel in terror? A genuine difference among scholars

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises an honest difficulty. The wording *kullu ummah*, "every community," means that the horrors of the Resurrection will be felt by all on the plain — believers and non-believers, righteous and unrighteous alike. Yet there are other verses and traditions that exclude the Prophets and the righteous from experiencing the horrors of the Plains of Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that the present verse is not in conflict with them, and offers three ways of reconciling the two:

1. **A moment so brief it is as if it never happened.** It is possible that the Prophets (peace be upon them) and the righteous will experience the horrors of the Plains of Resurrection for so short a period that the period will be as though it never existed.
2. ***Kull* here may mean "most," not "every."** The word is used that way occasionally in Arabic; on this reading the phrase would mean not all the people on the Plain of Resurrection but most people will experience the horror, and the Prophets and the righteous are excluded.
3. ***Jāthiyah* may describe the sitting posture of ṣalāh.** Some of the scholars take this position, and if it is taken for granted, the difficulty automatically disappears — because such a sitting is not out of fear or horror at all, but out of respect and honour.

These are the views as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents them; it does not force one on the reader, and neither should we. What all three share is the same underlying certainty: everyone is present, everyone is accountable, and the difference between people that Day is a difference in how they meet it.

## "Called to its record"

**"Each nation will be called to its Record."** Ibn Kathir explains *kitāb* simply: the Record of deeds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees that the word *kitāb*, according to most commentators, refers to the book of record which the angels have been writing in the world, and describes the scene: the record-books will be thrown on the Plains of Resurrection, and each one will receive his respective record-book, and it will be said to him, **"Read your book. This day you yourself are enough to take your own account"** (17:14). Being "called to the record-books," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, purports to say precisely this: that they will have to render an account of their deeds before Allah in the next life.

Ibn Kathir sets the verse beside its sisters. "And the Book will be presented; and the Prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward" (39:69). And then the line that follows here — **"This Day you shall be recompensed for what you used to do"** — which he glosses: you will be judged according to your deeds, good and evil. He also cites: "On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward, and what he left behind. Nay! Man will be a witness against himself, though he may put forth his excuses" (75:13–15).

That last verse is worth pausing on, because it names something we all recognise. A person can produce excuses — he may genuinely believe them — and still be, as the verse says, a witness against himself. The record does not create the truth; it confronts a person with it.

## Ayah 29: the record speaks

**"This, Our Record speaks about you with truth."** Ibn Kathir's comment is one line and it is the whole point: it contains the record of all your actions, **without addition or deletion**. Nothing flattering has been inserted; nothing embarrassing has been quietly dropped.

Notice the two words Allah attaches to the book. It is *"Our* Record" — not yours, not the angels' private notes, but Allah's own. And it *speaks*: it does not lie there to be interpreted or argued over. It testifies, *bi-l-ḥaqq*, with truth.

Ibn Kathir brings the scene from Sūrat al-Kahf to show what that testimony feels like from the wrong side: "And the Book will be presented, and you will see the criminals, fearful of that which is therein. They will say: 'Woe to us! What sort of Book is this that leaves neither a small thing nor a big thing, but has recorded it with numbers!' And they will find all that they did, placed before them, and your Lord treats no one with injustice" (18:49). Their cry is not "this is false." It is *"what sort of Book is this"* — astonishment at how complete it is. And the verse closes by shutting the last door: your Lord treats no one with injustice. There is no appeal on grounds of unfairness, because there is no unfairness.

## "We were recording what you used to do"

The final phrase, *innā kunnā nastansikh mā kuntum taʿmalūn*, Ibn Kathir explains as: 'We ordered Our scribe angels to record your deeds.' Ibn ʿAbbās and others then open up what that recording involves.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: the angels record the deeds of the servants and then ascend to heaven with them. There they meet the angels entrusted with the Records of deeds that are sent down from *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* on each Night of al-Qadr, containing what Allah has written will occur from the servants, long before He created them. The two are compared. And they find that **not a single letter was added or deleted.** Then he recited this very ayah.

Take in what that describes. Two records — one written by angels as a person lives, one containing what Allah had written long before that person existed at all — laid side by side, and matching to the letter. The book that will speak for or against you on that Day was never a surprise to the One who owns the heavens and the earth (ayah 27).

## Living it

**Your life is being written down as you live it.** Not weighed at the end from memory — recorded, as it happens, by scribe angels whom Allah ordered to record your deeds, and the Book that results misses nothing "small" and nothing "big" (18:49). The small things are named first in that verse, and that is where most of us leak: the remark, the glance, the quiet dishonesty nobody witnessed. Ibn Kathir's phrase is the standard to live against — *without addition or deletion*.

**Stop building a defence.** The Qurʼān has already told you the outcome of that project: a man may put forth his excuses and still be a witness against himself (75:13–15). The energy spent constructing a version of events is better spent changing the events.

**Nobody's credit transfers to you.** If Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, says "myself," and ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, will not raise the case of Maryam, then the question is not what your family, your teacher or your community has built. It is what is in *your* book.

**And there is mercy in the same verse.** A record kept "without addition or deletion" is terrifying only if you have something to hide from it. For someone who prayed when it was inconvenient, gave when nobody saw, held his tongue when he had every excuse to speak — this is the verse that guarantees none of it was mislaid. **"This Day you shall be recompensed for what you used to do."** The same exactness that exposes the deceiver vindicates the sincere. The kingdom belongs to Allah — and so does the ledger, and He treats no one with injustice.

passages.title: The two verdicts pronounced on Judgment Day
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the courtroom scene of Sūrat al-Jāthiyah reaching its verdict. Ibn Kathir introduces the whole block with a single sentence: here "Allah states to us His judgement in His creation on the Day of Resurrection." What holds ayat 30–35 together is one grammatical hinge — *fa-ammā… wa-ammā…*, "as for those… but as for those…" — which splits all of humanity into exactly two files. Ayah 30 disposes of the first group in one breath. Ayat 31–35 stay with the second group at length, because they are the ones who need to be shown, in their own remembered words, why the sentence is just.

The setting has already been described a little earlier in the surah: every community kneeling, and every community called to its book of record. That record, the Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is the book the angels were writing all along in this world; being "called to the book" means, in plain terms, that every soul will have to render an account of its deeds before Allah. Ayat 30–35 are the two sentences handed down once those books have been opened.

## The first verdict: admitted into His mercy (ayah 30)

"As for those who believed and did good deeds, their Lord will admit them to His mercy. That will be the evident success."

Ibn Kathir reads the two verbs as covering the whole person: **those whose hearts believed and whose limbs performed good deeds** — and he adds two conditions that govern the deeds, "in sincerity to Allah and conforming with Islamic legislation." Inward truthfulness and outward correctness. A deed done for Allah but invented in its form, or a deed correct in form but hollow in intention, is not what this ayah is describing.

Notice what they are admitted *into*. Not "into Paradise" — into **His mercy**. Ibn Kathir says plainly: "and that is Paradise." The renaming is the point. Paradise is not wages calculated and paid out; it is mercy, and the deeds are what mercy attaches itself to. Ibn Kathir cites a report found in the Sahih in which Allah said to Paradise:

> "You are My mercy, with which I grant mercy to whom I will."

Paradise *is* His mercy — that is its name from the other side.

Then the verdict is stamped: *dhālika huwa al-fawz al-mubīn* — "that will be the evident success." Ibn Kathir's gloss on *mubīn* is two words: "clear and apparent." Success that needs no argument, no spin, no comparison with anyone else's outcome. On that Day it will simply be visible.

## The second verdict: cross-examined by their own words (ayat 31–32)

"But as for those who disbelieved" — and then the ayah does not describe them, it *addresses* them. The switch from third person ("those who disbelieved") to second person ("Were not Our āyāt recited to **you**?") is the moment the reader is pulled into the dock. Ibn Kathir explains that they "will be admonished and criticized with this statement": have not the āyāt of ar-Raḥmān been recited to you? But you did not follow them out of pride and turned away upon hearing them.

Three charges are laid, and they escalate.

**One: pride.** *Fa-stakbartum* — "you were proud." Ibn Kathir puts his finger on the mechanism: the problem was never that the evidence failed to arrive. It arrived and was recited. The refusal came from arrogance, and arrogance expresses itself as turning away the moment you hear. It is worth sitting with the detail that Ibn Kathir supplies — these were "the āyāt of **ar-Raḥmān**", the Most Merciful. Mercy was speaking; pride would not sit still to listen.

**Two: criminality.** *Wa kuntum qawman mujrimīn* — "and you were a people who were criminals." Ibn Kathir specifies that this covers both layers: "by your actions, as well as, the denial that your hearts contained." Outward crime and inward denial, mirroring exactly the heart-and-limbs pairing that defined the believers in ayah 30. The two verdicts are built to the same blueprint.

**Three: treating the Hour as guesswork.** Ayah 32 recalls an actual exchange from worldly life. Ibn Kathir identifies the speakers: "when the believers said these words to you" — *inna waʿda-llāhi ḥaqq*, Allah's promise is the truth, and about the Hour there is no doubt. And here is the reply, quoted back to them:
