- *"Mā nadrī ma-s-sāʿah"* — "We know not what is the Hour." Ibn Kathir: 'we do not recognize what you are talking about.' A shrug dressed as intellectual honesty.
- *"In naẓunnu illā ẓannā"* — "we do not think it but conjecture." Ibn Kathir: 'we only remotely think that it might come.' Not flat denial — a maybe, held at arm's length.
- *"Wa mā naḥnu bi-mustayqinīn"* — "and we have no firm convincing belief." Ibn Kathir: 'we are not sure of it.'

This is the most searching part of the passage, because this is not the language of a defiant atheist. It is the language of a man who never quite got round to it. He does not deny the Hour; he declines to be certain about it. The ayah itself sets the two against each other — *ẓann*, a leaning guess, on one side, and being *mustayqin*, firmly convinced, on the other — and the force of ayat 31–32 is that a life run on a maybe was already a verdict being written.

## What surfaces and what closes in (ayah 33)

"And the evil of what they did will appear to them, and that which they used to mock at will completely encircle them."

Two verbs, moving in opposite directions and meeting on the same person.

*Badā lahum* — "will appear to them." Ibn Kathir: "the repercussion of their evil deeds will become apparent to them." What was buried in a lifetime, forgotten, explained away or genuinely lost from memory, now surfaces into view — the record of deeds finally rendered visible.

*Wa ḥāqa bihim* — "will completely encircle them." Ibn Kathir's gloss is one phrase, and it is the whole picture: **"from all directions."** No gap, no angle of escape. And what encircles them is precisely "that which they used to mock at" — Ibn Kathir specifies: "of the coming torment and punishment." The joke arrives in person and surrounds the one who told it. That exact reversal — the mocked thing becoming the encircling thing — is the passage's characteristic form of justice, and it is about to be applied once more.

## "This Day We will forget you" (ayah 34)

"And it will be said: 'This Day We will forget you as you forgot the meeting of this Day of yours. And your abode is the Fire, and there is none to help you.'"

This is the ayah that most needs care. Allah does not forget; forgetfulness is a deficiency, and He is far above it. Ibn Kathir gives the correct reading without any straining: *nansākum* means **"We will treat you as if We have forgotten you, casting you in the fire of Jahannam."** It is the language of consequence — being left, abandoned, unattended to — not of lapsed memory. As with all that Allah says of Himself, we affirm what He affirms as He intends it, without likening Him to His creation and without emptying His words of meaning.

And what exactly did they forget? Ibn Kathir is precise: they forgot "the meeting of this Day of yours" — meaning "and did not work for it because you did not believe in its coming." Forgetting here is not a memory failure either. It is the failure to *act* on something you were told. A man who never prepared for the meeting was, functionally, a man who had forgotten it.

Then the sentence closes: "And your abode is the Fire, and there is none to help you." Not one helper is left standing between them and what has been decided.

At this point Ibn Kathir brings a report from the Sahih, in which Allah the Exalted will question some of His servants on the Day of Resurrection:

> "Have I not given you a spouse, honored you and subjected the camels and horses to you? Have I not allowed you to be a chief and a master?" The servant will say in answer, "Yes, O Lord!" Allah will say, "Did you think that you would ever meet Me?" He will say, "No." Allah the Exalted will say, "then this Day, I will forget you as you forgot Me."

Read what that dialogue is made of. Marriage, honour, transport, standing among people — the ordinary furniture of a good life, itemised one by one, each admitted. Then a single question about whether any of it was ever understood as coming from Someone he would one day stand before. The gifts were received; the Giver was never expected. That is what "forgetting the meeting" looks like from the inside, and it is chillingly compatible with a comfortable, successful, respectable life.

## The two causes and the two closed doors (ayah 35)

"This, because you took the revelations of Allah in mockery, and the life of the world deceived you. So this Day, they shall not be taken out from there, nor shall they be returned to the worldly life."

*Dhālikum bi-annakum* — "this, because you…" The ayah does not merely sentence; it explains the sentence. Two causes are named.

**They took Allah's āyāt as a joke.** Ibn Kathir: 'We gave you this punishment as retribution because you mocked Allah's proofs that He sent to you, and made them the subject of jokes and jest.' Note that these are called *proofs*: the mockery was not aimed at something obscure but at evidence sent deliberately. Mockery is pride's public voice — the same arrogance of ayah 31, now with an audience.

**The life of the world deceived them.** *Gharratkum al-ḥayāt ad-dunyā.* Ibn Kathir: 'this life fooled you and you were seduced by it, thus becoming among the ultimate losers.' Being "fooled" and "seduced" is the language of a con, not a robbery. Nothing forced them; the world simply looked like enough, and they believed it.

Then two doors are shut in the same breath:

- *Fa-l-yawma lā yukhrajūna minhā* — "this Day they shall not be taken out from there," which Ibn Kathir specifies as **from Hellfire**. No exit forward.
- *Wa lā hum yustaʿtabūn* — Ibn Kathir renders this as "nor shall they be returned to the worldly life," and glosses: "no apologies shall be sought from them." No exit backward, and no appeals process. The time for offering an excuse and having it accepted was the time when the āyāt were being recited and they were turning away.

And then the closing comparison, which is where Ibn Kathir chooses to leave the whole scene: they "will be punished without limit or delay, **just as a group of the believers will enter Paradise without limit or delay**." The symmetry of *fa-ammā… wa-ammā* holds all the way to the end. Immediate on both sides.

## Where the passage is heading

Ibn Kathir observes that "after Allah mentioned His judgement for the believers and the disbelievers," the surah turns straight to praise, and then to Allah's majesty in the heavens and the earth — *al-kibriyā'*, which **Mujāhid** explained as *the kingship*. That single word closes a circle back to ayah 31. The disbelievers' ruin began with *istikbār* — making themselves big. Greatness, it turns out, was never an available position; it was already occupied. Ibn Kathir cites here an authentic hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ reported that Allah the Exalted said:

> "Glory is My robe and pride is My garment; whoever rivals Me for either of them, I will make him reside in My Fire!"

Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim collected a similar hadith. The Fire that ayah 34 named as the arrogant person's abode is here named as the destination of anyone who competes with Allah for what is His alone.

## Living it

The passage is unusually direct about what it asks, because every charge in it is something a believer can quietly fall into.

**Believe with the heart and work with the limbs.** Ayah 30 will not separate them, and Ibn Kathir's two conditions — sincerity to Allah, and conformity with what He legislated — are the test each deed has to pass twice.

**Do not run your life on *ẓann*.** The people of ayah 32 were not militant deniers. They said: we're not sure, it's only a guess. If the Hour is treated as a "probably" rather than a certainty, no work gets done for it — and ayah 34 defines exactly that as forgetting.

**Watch the reflex of turning away.** Ibn Kathir locates the disaster of ayah 31 not in ignorance but in pride reacting to a recitation. The āyāt still reach us; the only question is what happens in the heart in the second after they land.

**Never make a joke of Allah's āyāt.** Ayah 35 names this as the first cause of the sentence, and ayah 33 shows the mocked thing returning to encircle the mocker from every side.

**Name the deception for what it is.** *Gharratkum al-ḥayāt ad-dunyā* — the world does not usually attack faith; it simply offers itself as sufficient. The servant in the report from the Sahih had a spouse, honour, mounts and rank, and answered "Yes, O Lord" to every one of them. What he lacked was the expectation of meeting the One who gave them.

**Work for the meeting.** That is the single practical instruction hidden inside ayah 34. To remember the Day is to prepare for it; anything less, in this ayah's vocabulary, is called forgetting.

passages.title: Closing praise to the Lord of the worlds
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the closing seal of Sūrah al-Jāthiyah. After the long courtroom scene of the Day of Judgement — the believers ushered into mercy, the deniers shut into the Fire with no way out — the sūrah does not end with a warning or a plea. It ends with **praise**. What holds ayah 36 and 37 together is a single movement: because Allah's judgement is what it is, all praise belongs to Him (36); and because all majesty in the heavens and the earth is His alone, that praise is not flattery but plain fact (37).

## Praise placed exactly where it is placed

Ayah 36 opens with "So" — *So all praise is due to Allah.* Ibn Kathir marks the seam precisely: "After Allah mentioned His judgement for the believers and the disbelievers, He said: *So all praise is due to Allah…*"

So this is praise **as a verdict on the verdict**. Look at what has just been described in the ayat immediately before. In ayah 30, those who believed and did good deeds — Ibn Kathir explains this as "those whose hearts believed and their limbs performed good deeds, in sincerity to Allah and conforming with Islamic legislation" — are admitted by their Lord into His mercy, which Ibn Kathir identifies as Paradise. He cites a report in the Sahih in which Allah says to Paradise, "You are My mercy, with which I grant mercy to whom I will."

And in ayat 31–35, the other side: people who heard the ayat of Allah recited and turned away in pride; who, when told that Allah's promise is true and the Hour is beyond doubt, answered that they had only a vague guess about it and no firm conviction. Ibn Kathir renders their words from the inside — "we only remotely think that it might come… we are not sure of it." So on that Day it is said to them, "This Day We will forget you as you forgot the meeting of this Day of yours." Ibn Kathir is careful here: it means "We will treat you as if We have forgotten you, casting you in the fire of Jahannam" — for they "did not work for it because you did not believe in its coming." He cites a report in the Sahih in which Allah asks some of His servants on the Day of Resurrection: "Have I not given you a spouse, honoured you and subjected the camels and horses to you? Have I not allowed you to be a chief and a master?" The servant answers, "Yes, O Lord." Allah asks, "Did you think that you would ever meet Me?" He says, "No." And Allah says, "Then this Day, I will forget you as you forgot Me."

Then ayah 35 closes the door: they will not be taken out of the Fire, and — as Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase — "no apologies shall be sought from them, but they will be punished without limit or delay, just as a group of the believers will enter Paradise without limit or delay."

That is the scene. And the response the Qur'an teaches at the sight of it is *al-ḥamd*, praise. Praise, when everything has been weighed and nothing has been mishandled.

Nor is that praise shared out. Ibn Kathir's own closing words on this passage put it plainly: "all glory and praise are due to Him, none has the right to be worshipped but He, Alone."

## Three times "Lord"

The rest of ayah 36 turns on one word repeated three times: *Rabb*, Lord.

- Lord of the heavens
- and Lord of the earth
- Lord of all the worlds

*Rabb* here is not only "Lord" in the sense of a master one obeys. Ibn Kathir unpacks it as ownership and total charge: "He is their Owner and the Owner of all that is in and on them." The heavens, the earth, and everything held within them belong to Him as property belongs to its owner.

And notice that the ayah does not say it once. Each domain is named in turn and each one falls under Him — and then the third phrase, which Ibn Kathir renders "the Lord of all that exists," sweeps up anything a listener might have imagined was left outside. There is no second address to appeal to, no jurisdiction where the verdict of ayat 30–35 could be challenged. That is why the praise in this ayah is not sentimental. It rests on ownership.

## Ayah 37: the majesty that belongs to Him alone

"And His is the majesty in the heavens and the earth."

Ibn Kathir reports the interpretation of **Mujahid**, that the majesty spoken of here means **the kingship**. Majesty and sovereignty are one thing: to be truly great is to be the One who actually rules.

Ibn Kathir then draws out what the ayah is saying: "Allah is the Almighty, Worthy of all praise; everything and everyone is subservient and in complete need of and dependent upon Him." That last phrase is worth sitting with. Not "some things depend on Him" — everything, in complete need, always.

And here is the sharp edge of it. Look back at ayah 31, where the disbelievers are told, "Were not Our Ayat recited to you? But you were proud" — which Ibn Kathir paraphrases as, "you did not follow them out of pride and turned away upon hearing them." Pride is named as the thing that ruined them. Six ayat later the sūrah closes by declaring where majesty actually resides: with Allah, in the heavens and the earth. The passage names the disease and then names what the sick were reaching for.

Ibn Kathir cites at this ayah a ḥadīth he describes as authentic, in which the Prophet ﷺ reported that Allah the Exalted said: **"Glory is My robe and pride is My garment; whoever rivals Me for either of them, I will make him reside in My Fire."** Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim collected a similar ḥadīth.

The image is exact and terrifying. A robe and an outer garment are what one person wears and no one else puts on. Greatness is not something Allah possesses among other possessors of it; the ḥadīth pictures it as clothing that is His alone. To contest it is not merely rude — it is to reach for what cannot be shared, and the ḥadīth names the consequence without softening it.

**A word on belief here.** We affirm greatness, majesty and kingship for Allah exactly as He and His Messenger ﷺ described them — real attributes, truly His — without imagining them to resemble anything in creation, and without emptying the words of meaning. The robe and the garment in the ḥadīth convey how exclusively greatness belongs to Him; they say nothing about His being resembling ours. He is as He described Himself, and nothing in creation is like Him.

## Al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥakīm

The sūrah closes on two of Allah's names, and Ibn Kathir gives each a compact gloss:

**Al-ʿAzīz** — the Almighty, the One "who is never resisted or rivalled." Power that meets no successful opposition anywhere. Nothing in the scene of Judgement was carried out over any objection that could stand.

**Al-Ḥakīm** — "all wise in His statements, actions, legislation and the decree that He appoints." Four arenas: what He says, what He does, what He commands of us, and what He decrees for us. Wisdom in all four.

Put the two names side by side and you have the answer to every quiet complaint the human heart raises about the Last Day. *Al-ʿAzīz* means He is able to do whatever He wills; *al-Ḥakīm* means that what He wills is never arbitrary. Overwhelming power without wisdom would be tyranny; wisdom without power would be helpless good intention. He is both — and that is precisely why the fitting response in ayah 36 was praise and not protest.

## Living it

**Praise is the believer's posture toward the outcome, not only the gift.** The sūrah does not place *al-ḥamd* after a description of rain or provision. It places it after Hell is sealed and Paradise is opened. Learning to say *alḥamdulillāh* over Allah's decisions — including the ones that are severe — is what these ayat train.

**Guard yourself from the sin this passage names.** Pride destroyed the people of ayah 31: they heard the ayat and, in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase, "did not follow them out of pride and turned away upon hearing them." Ayah 37 shows why that is fatal: majesty in the heavens and the earth is His, not ours. Practically, this shows up in small refusals — refusing to accept a clear proof because of who said it, refusing to climb down from a position, needing to be seen as the greatest in the room. The ḥadīth of the robe and the garment treats that as a contest with Allah.

**Take the Hour seriously as a certainty, not a guess.** The condemned in ayah 32 did not deny the Hour outright; they said, "We do not think it but conjecture, and we have no firm convincing belief." Ibn Kathir's paraphrase — "we only remotely think that it might come" — is uncomfortably close to how many people actually live. The cure is not more information; it is *working for that Day*, since Ibn Kathir ties their forgetting precisely to their not working for it: they "did not work for it because you did not believe in its coming."

**Let dependence be conscious.** If "everything and everyone is subservient and in complete need of and dependent upon Him," then supplication is not an unusual act. It is simply telling the truth about your situation.

## How the commentators themselves closed

There is something quietly beautiful in how the classical scholars end their treatment of this sūrah. Ibn Kathir finishes: "This is the end of the Tafsir of Sūrat al-Jāthiyah. All praise and thanks are due to Allah alone." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends with a single word — *Alhamdulillah* — and then, "The Commentary on Surah al-Jathiyah ends here."

They close their books the way the sūrah closes itself. Ayah 36 taught them the last word, and they used it.

And so the sūrah ends where every account of the Day of Judgement should end — not in argument, not in dread, but in the only thing left to say. All praise is for Allah, Lord of the heavens, Lord of the earth, Lord of all the worlds; His is the majesty; and He is al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥakīm.
